name: Lucillius
bio: Lucillius, a Greek epigrammatist of the first century AD, is one of the Anthology's satirical writers; not to be confused with the Roman satirist Lucilius.
Paton's first volume ascribes one epigram to him without qualification, a dedication in Book VI.

poems.title: Book VI, 166
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Dionysius, the only one saved out of forty sailors, dedicated here the image of his hydrocele, tying which close to his thighs he swam to shore. So even a hydrocele brings luck on some occasions.

poems.title: Book IX, 55
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.note: Also attributed to Menecrates of Samos.
poems.text: If anyone who has reached old age prays for life, he deserves to go on growing old for many decades.

poems.title: Book IX, 572
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: “Let us begin our song from the Heliconian Muses”; so Hesiod wrote, they say, while he kept his sheep. “Sing, O goddess, the wrath,” and “Tell me, Muse, the man,” said Calliope by the mouth of Homer. Now I have got to write a proem of some sort. But what shall I write now I am beginning to publish this second book? “Olympian Muses, daughters of Zeus, I should not have been saved unless Nero Caesar had given me money.”

poems.title: Book X, 122
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Heaven can do many things even though they be unlikely ; it exalteth the little and casteth down the great. Thy lofty looks and pride it shall make to cease, even though a river bring thee streams of gold. The wind hurts not the rush or the mallow, but the greatest oaks and planes it can lay low on the ground.

poems.title: Book XI, 10
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: You know the rule of my little banquets. To-day, Aulus, I invite you under new convivial laws. No lyric poet shall sit there and recite, and you yourself shall neither trouble us nor be troubled with literary discussions.

poems.title: Book XI, 11
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: I never knew, Epicrates, that you were a tragedian or a choral flute-player or any other sort of person whose business it is to have a chorus with them. But I invited you alone; you, however, came bringing with you from home a chorus of dancing slaves, to whom you hand all the dishes over your shoulder as a gift. If this is to be so, make the slaves sit down at table and we will come and stand at their feet to serve.

poems.title: Book XI, 68
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Some say, Nicylla, that you dye your hair, but you bought it as black as coal in the market.

poems.title: Book XI, 69
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Themistonoe, three times a crow’s age, when she dyes her grey hair becomes suddenly not young (nea) but Rhea.

poems.title: Book XI, 75
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: This Olympicus who is now such as you see him, Augustus, once had a nose, a chin, a forehead, ears and eyelids. Then becoming a professional boxer he lost all, not even getting his share of his father’s inheritance ; for his brother presented a likeness of him he had and he was pronounced to be a stranger, as he bore no resemblance to it.

poems.title: Book XI, 76
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Having such a mug, Olympicus, go not to a fountain nor look into any transparent water, for you, like Narcissus, seeing your face clearly, will die, hating yourself to the death.

poems.title: Book XI, 77
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: When Ulysses after twenty years came safe to his home, Argos the dog recognised his appearance when he saw him, but you, Stratophon, after boxing for four hours, have become not only unrecognisable to dogs but to the city. If you will trouble to look at your face in a glass, you will say on your oath, “I am not Stratophon.”’

poems.title: Book XI, 78
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Your head, Apollophanes, has become a sieve, or the lower edge of a worm-eaten book, all exactly like ant-holes, crooked and straight, or musical notes Lydian and Phrygian. But go on boxing without fear ; for even if you are struck on the head you will have the marks you have—you can’t have more.

poems.title: Book XI, 79
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Cleombrotus ceased to be a pugilist, but afterwards married and now has at home all the blows of the Isthmian and Nemean games, a pugnacious old woman hitting as hard as in the Olympian fights, and he dreads his own house more than he ever dreaded the ring. Whenever he gets his wind, he is beaten with all the strokes known in every match to make him pay her his debt!; and if he pays it, he is beaten again.

poems.title: Book XI, 80
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: His competitors set up here the statue of Apis the boxer, for he never hurt anyone.

poems.title: Book XI, 81
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: I, Androleos, took part in every boxing contest that the Greeks preside over, every single one. At Pisa I saved one ear, and in Plataea one eyelid, but at Delphi I was carried out insensible. Damoteles, my father, and my fellow-townsmen had been summoned by herald to bear me out of the stadion either dead or mutilated.

poems.title: Book XI, 83
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Or late the great earth made everything quake, but only the runner Erasistratus it did not move from his place.

poems.title: Book XI, 84
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: None among the competitors was thrown quicker than myself and none ran the race slower. With the quoit I never came near the rest, I never was able to lift my legs for a jump and a cripple could throw the javelin better than I. I am the first who out of the five events was proclaimed beaten in all five.’

poems.title: Book XI, 85
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Marcus once running in armour, went on until it was midnight, so that the course was closed on all sides ; for the public servants all thought that he was one of the honorary stone statues of men in armour set up there. What happened? Why next year they opened, and Marcus came in, but a whole stadion behind.

poems.title: Book XI, 87
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: The house five fathoms long had room for tall Timomachus if he always lay on the floor ; but if he ever wanted to stand, his slaves had to bore a hole in the roof in the morning five feet by five.

poems.title: Book XI, 88
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: A gnat carried off little Erotion as she was playing. “ What is going to happen to me ?” she said, “ Dost thou want me, father Zeus ?”’

poems.title: Book XI, 89
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Short Hermogenes when he lets anything fall on the ground pulls it down with a halbert.

poems.title: Book XI, 90
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Do you know, Dionysius, that little Marcus, being angry with his father, set on end a probe and hanged himself on it.

poems.title: Book XI, 91
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Thin Stratonicus fixed on a reed a spike of corn and attaching himself to it by a hair hanged himself. And what happened? He was not heavy enough to hang down, but his dead body flies in the air above his gallows, although there is no wind.

poems.title: Book XI, 92
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Lean Gaius, when he breathed his last yesterday, left absolutely nothing to be carried to the grave, and finally going down to Hades just as he was when alive flutters there the thinnest of the skeletons under earth. His kinsmen bore on their shoulders his empty bier, writing above it “This is the funeral of Gaius.”

poems.title: Book XI, 93
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Lean Marcus once made a hole with his head in one of Epicurus’ atoms and went through the middle of it.

poems.title: Book XI, 94
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Lean Marcus sounding a trumpet just blew into it and went straight headforemost down it.

poems.title: Book XI, 95
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: A small mouse finding little Macron asleep one summer’s day dragged him into its hole by his foot. But he in the hole, though unarmed, strangled the mouse and said, “ Father Zeus, thou hast a second Heracles.”

poems.title: Book XI, 99
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: As thin little Proclus was blowing the fire the smoke took him up and went off with him from here through the window. With difficulty he swum to a cloud and came down through it wounded in a thousand places by the atomies.

poems.title: Book XI, 100
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Gaius was so very light that he used to dive with a stone or lead hung from his foot.

poems.title: Book XI, 101
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Demetrius, fanning slight little Artemidora in her sleep, fanned her off the roof.”

poems.title: Book XI, 103
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Epicurus wrote that all the world consisted of atoms, thinking, Alcimus, that an atom was the most minute thing. But if Diophantus had existed then he would have written that it consisted of Diophantus, who is much more minute than the atoms. Or he would have written that other things were composed of atoms, but the atoms themselves, Alcimus, of Diophantus.

poems.title: Book XI, 104
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Poor Menestratus once, riding on an ant as if it were ‘an elephant, was suddenly stretched on his back. When it trod on him and he was breathing his last, “O Envy!” he exclaimed, “thus riding perished Phaethon too.”

poems.title: Book XI, 105
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: I was looking for great Eumecius, and he was asleep with his arms stretched out under a small saucer.

poems.title: Book XI, 106
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Chaeremon caught by a slight breeze was floating in the air, much lighter than a straw. He would soon have been swept away through the air, if he had not caught his feet in a spider’s web and hung there on his back. Here he hung for five days and nights, and on the sixth day came down by a thread of the web.

poems.title: Book XI, 107
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Chaeremon fell flat on his back, struck by a poplar leaf carried by the wind, and he lies on the ground like Tityus or rather like a caterpillar, stretching on the ground his skeleton body.

poems.title: Book XI, 131
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Nor water in Deucalion’s day when all became water, nor Phaethon who burned up the inhabitants of the earth, slew so many men as Potamon the poet and Hermogenes by his surgery killed. So from the beginning of the ages there have been these four curses, Deucalion, Phaethon, Hermogenes and Potamon.

poems.title: Book XI, 132
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: I hate, Lord Caesar, those who are never pleased with any young writer, even if he says “Sing, O Goddess, the wrath,’ but if a man is not as old as Priam, if he is not half bald and not so very much bent, they say he can’t write abc. But, Zeus most high, if this really be so, wisdom visits but the ruptured.

poems.title: Book XI, 133
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Eutychides the lyric poet is dead. Fly, ye people who dwell under earth ; Eutychides is coming with odes, and he ordered them to burn with him twelve lyres and twenty-five cases of music. Now indeed Charon has got hold of you. Where can one depart to in future, since Eutychides is established in Hades too?

poems.title: Book XI, 134
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Shall we begin, Heliodorus? Shall we play thus at these poems together? Do you wish it, Heliodorus? “Come near, that swifter thou mayst reach Death’s goal” ; for you will see in me a master of tedious twaddle more Heliodorian than yourself.

poems.title: Book XI, 135
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: No longer, Marcus, no longer lament the boy, but me, who am much more dead than that child of yours. Make elegies, hangman, now for me, make dirges for me who am slain by this very death. For all for the sake of that dead child of yours I suffer what I would the inventors of books and pens might suffer.

poems.title: Book XI, 136
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: No sword so maleficent was ever forged by man for sudden treacherous attack as is the undeclared war of murderous hexameters, Callistratus, that you come to wage with me. Sound the retreat on the bugle at once, for even Priam by his tears gained his foes’ consent (?) to an armistice.

poems.title: Book XI, 137
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: You serve me a slice of raw beef, Heliodorus, and pour me out three cups of wine rawer than the beef, and then you wash me out at once with epigrams. If sinning against heaven I have eaten one of the oxen from Trinacria, I would like to gulp down the sea at once—but if the sea is too far from here, take me up and throw me into a well.

poems.title: Book XI, 138
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: If I only think of the grammarian Heliodorus, my tongue at once commits solecisms and I suffer from impediment of speech.

poems.title: Book XI, 139
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Zenonis keeps Menander the bearded grammar-teacher, and says she has entrusted her son to him; but he never stops at night making her practise cases, conjunctions, figures, and conjugations.

poems.title: Book XI, 140
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: To these praters, these verse-fighters of the supper table, these slippery dominies of Aristarchus’ school who care not for making a joke or drinking, but lie there playing infantile games with Nestor and Priam, cast me not literally “to be their prey and spoil.’? To-day I don’t sup on ‘Sing, O Goddess, the wrath.”

poems.title: Book XI, 141
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: I tosr a little pig and a cow and one nanny-goat, and on account of them you received your little fee, ‘ He is here ridiculing rhetors who ornamented their speeches with phrases from Demosthenes and the old orators. Menecles. I never had anything in common with Othryades nor do I prosecute the three hundred from Thermopylae for theft; my suit is against Eutychides, so that here how do Xerxes and the Spartans help me? I beg you just to mention me for form’s sake, or I will call out loud “One thing says Menecles, and another thing says the piggie.”’

poems.title: Book XI, 142
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: After having studied “Far be it,” and sphin and thrice in each period, “ Gentlemen of the jury,” and “ Here, usher, repeat the law for me,” and “ This way, and “I put it to you,’ and “ two score,” and “certain alleged,’ and indeed “ By heaven,” and «’Sdeath,”’ Crito is an orator and teaches numbers of children, and to these phrases he will add gru,’ phathi, and min.

poems.title: Book XI, 143
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Piutro will not receive the rhetor Marcus when dead, saying, “Let our one dog Cerberus be enough here ; but if thou wilt come in at any cost, declaim to Ixion, Melito‘ the lyric poet, and Tityus. For I have no evil worse than thee, until the day when Rufus the grammarian shall come here with his solecisms.”’

poems.title: Book XI, 148
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Flaccus the rhetor made solecisms the other day without even speaking, and when he was about to yawn at once was guilty of a barbarism, and now goes on making solecisms by signs with his hand, and I, seeing him, am tongue-tied.

poems.title: Book XI, 153
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: No one at all denies, Menestratus, that you are a cynic and bare-footed and that you are shivering. But if you shamelessly steal loaves and broken pieces on the sly, I have a stick, and they call you a dog.

poems.title: Book XI, 154
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Everyone who is poor and illiterate does not grind corn as formerly or carry burdens for small pay, but grows a beard and picking up a stick from the cross-roads, calls himself the chief dog of virtue. This is the sage pronouncement of Hermodotus, “ If anyone is penniless, let him throw off his shirt and no longer starve.”

poems.title: Book XI, 155
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: “This solid adamant of virtue, this rebuker of everyone, this fighter with the cold, with his long beard, has been caught.” “ At what?” “It is not proper to say at what, but he was caught doing things that foul-mouthed people do.”

poems.title: Book XI, 159
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: All the astrologers as it were with one voice prophesied to my father a ripe old age for his brother. Hermoclides alone foretold his premature death, but he foretold it when we were lamenting over his corpse in the house.

poems.title: Book XI, 160
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: All those who take horoscopes from observing Mars and Saturn are deserving of one cudgelling. I shall see them perhaps at no distant date really learning what a bull can do and how strong a lion is.

poems.title: Book XI, 161
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Onesimus the boxer came to the prophet Olympus wishing to learn if he were going to live to old age. And he said, “ Yes, if you give up the ring now, but if you go on boxing, Saturn is your horoscope.”

poems.title: Book XI, 163
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Onesimus the wrestler and the pentathlist Hylas and the runner Menecles came to the prophet Olympus wishing to know which of them was going to win at the games, and he, after inspecting the sacrifice, said, “ You will all win—unless anyone passes you, Sir, or unless anyone throws you, Sir, or unless anyone runs past you, Sir.”

poems.title: Book XI, 164
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Aulus the astrologer, after making out his own nativity, said that the fatal hour had come and that he had still four hours to live. When it reached the fifth hour and he had to go on living convicted of ignorance, he grew ashamed of Petosiris and hanged himself, and there up in the air he is dying, but he is dying ignorant.

poems.title: Book XI, 165
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Criro the miser, when he has a pain in his stomach refreshes himself by smelling not mint, but a penny piece.

poems.title: Book XI, 171
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Hermocrates the miser when he was dying wrote himself his own heir in his will, and he lay there reckoning what fee he must pay the doctors if he leaves his bed and how much his illness costs him. But when he found it cost one drachma more if he were saved, “It pays,” he said, “to die,” and stiffened himself out. Thus he lies, having nothing but an obol, and his heirs were glad to seize on his wealth.

poems.title: Book XI, 172
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Autus the miser drowned in the sea a child that was born to him, reckoning how much it would cost him if he kept it.

poems.title: Book XI, 174
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Dio yesterday stole Cypris all of gold, just risen from her mother sea, and he also pulled down with his hand Adonis of beaten gold and the little Love that stood by. Even the best thieves that ever were will now say, “ No longer do we enter into a contest of dexterity with you.”

poems.title: Book XI, 175
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Eutychides stole the god himself by whom he was about to swear, saying, “ I can’t swear by you.”

poems.title: Book XI, 176
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: As he carried off the winged Hermes, the servant of the gods, the Lord of the Arcadians, the cattle-raider, who stood here as curator of this gymnasium, Aulus the night-thief said, “ Many pupils are cleverer than their teachers.”

poems.title: Book XI, 177
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Eutychides stole Phoebus the detector of thieves, saying, “Speak not too much, but compare thy art with mine and thy oracles with my hands and a prophet with a thief and a god with Eutychides. And because of thy unbridled tongue thou shalt be sold at once, and then say of me what thou wilt to thy purchasers.”

poems.title: Book XI, 178
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Herdsman, feed thy flock far away, lest Pericles the thief drive thee and thy cattle off together.

poems.title: Book XI, 179
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: If Dio had feet like his hands, Dio, and Hermes no longer, would be distinguished among men as winged.

poems.title: Book XI, 183
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Heliodorus, hearing that Saturn troubles nativities, carried off the golden Saturn at night from the temple, saying: “Experience by fact, my Lord, which of us anticipated the other in working evil, and thou shalt know which of us is the Saturn of which. ‘Who works evil for another, works it for his own heart.’ Fetch me a good price and portend what thou wilt by thy rising.”

poems.title: Book XI, 184
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: From the Hesperides’ Garden of Zeus, Meniscus, as Heracles did formerly, carried off three golden apples. Well, what happened ? When he was caught he became a famous spectacle for all, burning alive, like Heracles of old.

poems.title: Book XI, 185
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Hecetocuus, my Lord Caesar, once emptied a Greek city by appearing to sing the part of Nauplius. Nauplius is ever an evil to the Greeks, either sending a great wave on their ships or having a lyre-singer to play his part.

poems.title: Book XI, 189
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Apollophanes the tragedian sold for five obols the stage property of five gods, the club of Heracles, Tisiphone’s instruments of terror, the trident of Poseidon, the shield of Athena, and the quiver of Artemis. “And the gods that sit beside Zeus ” were stripped to get a few coppers to buy a little bread and wine.

poems.title: Book XI, 190
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: The barber is puzzled to know where to begin to shave the head of hairy Hermogenes, as he seems to be all head.

poems.title: Book XI, 191
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: “ Ares, Ares, destroyer of men, blood-fiend,” cease, barber, from cutting me, for you have no place left in which to cut me. But change now to my muscles and my legs below the knees, and cut me there, and I will let you. For even now the shop is full of flies, and if you persist, you will see the tribes of vultures and ravens here.

poems.title: Book XI, 192
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Envious Diophon, seeing another man near him crucified on a higher cross than himself, fell into a decline.

poems.title: Book XI, 194
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: To Pan who loves the cave, and the Nymphs that haunt the hills, and to the Satyrs and to the holy Hamadryads within the cave, Marcus..., having killed nothing with his dogs and boar-spears, hung up the dogs themselves.

poems.title: Book XI, 196
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Biro, with a face three times worse than a monkey’s, enough to make even Hecate hang herself for envy if she saw it, says, “I am chaste, Lucilius, and sleep alone ;” for perhaps she is ashamed of saying “I am a virgin.” But may whoever hates me marry such a horror and have children of similar chastity.

poems.title: Book XI, 197
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Hieronymus formerly wanted to be too drimys (strict) ; now he has the drz, but the mys has turned into los. The complainant here had been dancing in the pantomime the part of Hyrnetho.

poems.title: Book XI, 205
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Eutychides when he came to supper, Dionysius, did not leave Aulus a single scrap, but handed everything to his servant behind him, and now Eutychides has a great supper in his house, and Aulus, not invited, sits eating dry bread.”

poems.title: Book XI, 206
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: So may you be able, Dionysius, to digest all these things you are eating, but for custom’s sake give us something to eat here too. I was invited also, and Publius served some of these things for me too to taste, and my portion too is on the board. Unless, seeing that I am thin, you think I was ill when I sat down to table, and so watch me thus in case I eat something unnoticed by you.

poems.title: Book XI, 207
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: You eat as much as five wolves, Gamus, and you hand to your slave behind you all that is over, not only your own portion, but that of those round you. But come to-morrow with your slave’s basket, and bring sawdust and a sponge and a broom.

poems.title: Book XI, 208
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: As a racer Eutychides was slow, but he ran to supper so quickly that they said, “ Eutychides is flying.”

poems.title: Book XI, 210
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Aulus the soldier stops his ears when he sees charcoal or laurel, wrapping his yellow duds tight round his head, and he shudders at his own useless sword ; and if you ever say, “They are coming,” he falls flat on his back. No Polemo or Stratoclides will he approach, but always has Lysimachus for a friend.”

poems.title: Book XI, 211
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: When Calpurnius the soldier saw the battle by the ships painted on a wall, as is the custom, the warrior lay stretched out pulseless and pale, calling out, “ Quarter, ye Trojans dear to Ares.” Then he enquired if he had been wounded, and with difficulty believed he was alive when he had agreed to pay ransom to the wall.

poems.title: Book XI, 212
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: I ordered you, Diodorus, to paint a pretty child, but you produce a child strange to me, putting a dog’s head on his shoulders, so that I weep to think how my Zopyrion was born to me by Hecuba. And finally I, Erasistratus the butcher, have got for six drachmae a son Anubis from the shrines of Isis.

poems.title: Book XI, 214
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Having painted Deucalion and Phaethon, Menestratus, you enquire which of them is worth anything. We will appraise them according to their own fate. Phaethon is truly worthy of the fire and Deucalion of the water.

poems.title: Book XI, 215
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Eutychus the painter was the father of twenty sons, but never got a likeness even among his children.

poems.title: Book XI, 216
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: You have heard of Cratippus as a lover of boys. It is a great marvel I have to tell you, but great goddesses are the Avengers. We discovered that Cratippus, the lover of boys, belongs now to another variety of those persons whose tastes lie in an inverse direction. Would I ever have expected this? I expected it, Cratippus. Shall I go mad because, while you told everyone you were a wolf, you suddenly turned out to be a kid?

poems.title: Book XI, 217
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: To avoid suspicion, Apollophanes married and walked as a bridegroom through the middle of the market, saying, “To-morrow at once I will have a child.” Then when to-morrow came he appeared carrying the suspicion instead of a child.

poems.title: Book XI, 233
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Phaedrus the man of business and the painter Rufus contended as to which of them would copy quickest and most truly. But while Rufus was about to mix his paints Phaedrus took and wrote out a renouncement of Rufus’ claim faithful as a picture.

poems.title: Book XI, 234
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: If Craterus’ feet and hands were sound, his head was not, when he wrote such stuff.

poems.title: Book XI, 239
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Not Homer’s Chimaera breathed such foul breath, not the fire-breathing herd of bulls of which they tell, not all Lemnos nor the excrements of the Harpies, nor Philoctetes’ putrefying foot. So that in universal estimation, Telesilla, you surpass Chimerae, rotting sores, bulls, birds, and the women of Lemnos.

poems.title: Book XI, 240
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Demostratis not only breathes herself the stink of a he-goat, but makes those who smell her breathe the same.

poems.title: Book XI, 245
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: The sides of the ship, Diophantes, let in all the waves, and through the ports ocean enters; and we see Swimming in your ship herds of dolphins and the bright children of Nereus. But if we wait longer someone will soon be sailing inside this our ship, for there is no more water left in the sea.

poems.title: Book XI, 246
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: From what quarry, Dionysius, did you hew these timbers? Of what mill-stones is the ship built? For if I know anything about it, it is a kind of lead, not oak or pine, and the lower part of me is nearly taking root. Perhaps I shall suddenly become a stone; and then the worst of it is Melito will write a rotten drama about me as if I were Niobe.

poems.title: Book XI, 247
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Or a truth, Dionysius, we the seas sail, and the ship is full of every sea from all parts. The Adriatic, the Tyrrhene Sea, the Gulf of Issa, the Aegean, are running dry. This is no ship, but a wooden fountain of ocean. To arms, Caesar! Dionysius begins already not to command a ship, but to command the seas.

poems.title: Book XI, 249
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Menophanes bought a field, and from hunger hanged himself on another man’s oak. When he was dead they had no earth to throw over him from above, but he was buried for payment in the ground of one of his neighbours. If Epicurus had known of Menophanes’ field he would have said that everything is full of fields, not of atoms.

poems.title: Book XI, 253
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: From what oak-trees did your father cut you, Aristo, or from what mill-stone quarry did he hew you? For indeed you are a dancer “ made of a venerable tree or of stone,” the living original of Niobe; so that I wonder and say: “You, too, must have had some quarrel with Leto, or else you would not have been naturally made of stone.”

poems.title: Book XI, 254
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: You played in the ballet everything according to the story, but by overlooking one very important action you highly displeased us. Dancing the part of Niobe you stood like a stone, and again when you were Capaneus‘ you suddenly fell down. But in the ease of Canace you were not clever, for you had a sword, but yet left the stage alive; that was not according to the story.

poems.title: Book XI, 256
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: They say you spend a long time in the bath, Heliodora, an old woman of a hundred not yet retired from the profession. But I know why you do it. You hope to grow young, like old Pelias, by being boiled.

poems.title: Book XI, 257
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Diophantus saw Hermogenes the doctor in his sleep and never woke up again, although he was wearing an amulet.

poems.title: Book XI, 258
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Autus the boxer dedicates to the Lord of Pisa his skull, having collected the bones one by one. And if he escapes from Nemea, Lord Zeus, he will perchance dedicate to thee also the vertebrae he still has left.

poems.title: Book XI, 259
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: You have a Thessalian horse, Erasistratus, but all the magic of Thessaly cannot make him stir; truly a wooden horse which would never have got through the Scaean gates, if all the Trojans and Greeks together had dragged it. If you take my advice, put him up as a votive statue to some god and make his barley into gruel for your children.

poems.title: Book XI, 264
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Hermon the miser, having spent money in his sleep, hanged himself from vexation.

poems.title: Book XI, 265
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: If an army is being led against locusts, or dog-flies, or mice, or the cavalry of fleas or frogs, you too should be afraid, Gaius, of someone enrolling you as being worthy of fighting with such foes. But if an army of brave men is being despatched, amuse yourself with something else; but the Romans do not fight against cranes.

poems.title: Book XI, 266
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Demosthenes has a lying mirror, for if she saw the truth she would not want to look into it at all.

poems.title: Book XI, 276
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Impotent Marcus once, when cast into prison, confessed to a murder of his own accord, being too lazy to come out.

poems.title: Book XI, 277
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Lazy Marcus, having once run in his sleep, never went to sleep again lest he should chance to run once more.

poems.title: Book XI, 278
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Outside you teach the woes of Paris and Menelaus, having at home plenty of Parises for your Helen.

poems.title: Book XI, 279
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: None of the grammarians can ever be moderate, as from the very beginning he has wrath, and spite, and bile.

poems.title: Book XI, 294
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Thou hast the wealth of a rich man, but the soul of a pauper, thou who art rich for thy heirs and poor for thyself.

poems.title: Book XI, 295
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: If thou hast any Dionysus in thy house, take off the ivy from his head and crown him with lettuce leaves.

poems.title: Book XI, 308
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Lean Cleonicus, making a hole in his foot with the needle, himself made a hole in the needle with his foot.

poems.title: Book XI, 309
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Thrasymachus, you lost great wealth by a plot, and, poor fellow, you have suddenly come to naught after all your economising, lending, exacting interest, drinking water, often not even eating, so as to have a little more money. But if you calculate what starvation was then and what it is now, you have no less now than you then seemed to have.

poems.title: Book XI, 310
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: You bought hair, rouge, honey, wax, and teeth. For the same outlay you might have bought a face.

poems.title: Book XI, 311
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Pantaenetus is so lazy that when he fell sick of a fever he prayed to every god never to get up again. And now he leaves his bed unwillingly, and in his heart blames the deaf ears of the unjust gods.

poems.title: Book XI, 312
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Though there is no one dead here now, O passer-by, Marcus the poet built a tomb here, and writing an inscription of one line as follows, engraved it : “Weep for twelve year old Maximus from Ephesus.” I (says the tomb) never even saw any Maximus, but to show off the poet’s talent I bid the passer-by weep.

poems.title: Book XI, 313
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: One, bidding me to a banquet, killed me with silver hunger, serving famished dishes. And in wrath I spoke amid the silver sheen of hunger: “ Where is the plenty of my earthenware dishes?”

poems.title: Book XI, 314
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: I soucur whence I should say the word. pinakes (dishes) was derived, and on being invited by you I found out why they are so called. For you placed before me great pinakes of great peina (hunger), famished dishes, instruments of famine.

poems.title: Book XI, 315
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Antiochus once set eyes on Lysimachus’ cushion, and Lysimachus never set eyes on it again.

poems.title: Book XI, 388
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: As long as you are unmarried, Numenius, everything in life seems to you the best of the best, but when a wife enters the house everything again in life seems to you at once the worst of the worst. “ But I marry for the sake of having children,” says he. You will have children, Numenius, if you have money, but a poor man does not even love his children.

poems.title: Book XI, 389
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: If thou livest the long years of a stag or crow thou mayest be pardoned for amassing vast wealth, but if thou art one of mortal men, whom old age right soon assails, let not the furious desire of immeasurable possessions beset thee, lest thou destroy thy soul in insufferable torture and others use thy goods without toiling for them.

poems.title: Book XI, 390
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: If thou lovest me, love me indeed, and do me no evil, making friendship the beginning of injury. For will have children—people running after your money and wishing you to adopt them; but if poor and married, your children will be a source of trouble. I say that for all men open enmity is much better than deceptive friendship. They say, too, that for seafaring ships sunken reefs are worse than visible rocks.

poems.title: Book XI, 391
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Asclepiades the miser saw a mouse in his house and said: “ My dearest mouse, what business have you here with me?” And the mouse said, smiling sweetly: “Fear nothing, my friend, I do not seek board with you, but residence.”

poems.title: Book XI, 392
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: Adrastus the rhetor, seating himself on the back of a winged ant, spoke as follows: “Fly, O Pegasus, thou hast thy Bellerophon.” Yes indeed the most doughty of heroes, a half-dead skeleton?

poems.title: Book XI, 393
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: There is no greater burden than a daughter, and ‘if, Euctemon, you think it is a light one, listen to me. You have a hydrocele and I have a daughter ; take her and give me a hundred hydroceles instead of one.

poems.title: Book XI, 394
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text: He is really the most excellent of poets who gives supper to those who have listened to his recitation. But if he reads to them and sends them home fasting, let him turn his own madness on his own head.

poems.title: Popular Songs (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Eutychides, the writer of songs, is dead; flee, O you under earth! Eutychides is coming with his odes; he left instructions to burn along with him twelve lyres and twenty-five boxes of airs. Now Charon has come upon you; whither may one retreat in future, since Eutychides fills Hades too?

poems.title: Grammar, Music, Rhetoric (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Pluto turns away the dead rhetorician Marcus, saying, "Let the dog Cerberus suffice us here; yet if thou needs must, declaim to Ixion and Melito the song-writer, and Tityus; for I have no worse evil than thee, till Rufus the critic comes to murder the language here."

poems.title: An Ungrounded Scandal (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Some say, Nicylla, that you dye your hair; which is as black as can be bought in the market.

poems.title: The Fortunate Painter (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Eutychus the portrait-painter got twenty sons, and never got one likeness, even among his children.

poems.title: Marcus the Runner (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Marcus once saw midnight out in the armed men's race, so that the race-course was all locked up, as the police all thought that he was one of the stone men in armour who stand there in honour of victors. Very well, it was opened next day, and then Marcus turned up, still short of the goal by the whole course.

poems.title: Hermogenes (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Little Hermogenes, when he lets anything fall on the ground, has to drag it down to him with a hook at the end of a pole.

poems.title: Phantasms of the Living (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Lean Gaius yesterday breathed his very last breath, and left nothing at all for burial, but having passed down into Hades just as he was in life, flutters there the thinnest of the anatomies under earth; and his kinsfolk lifted an empty bier on their shoulders, inscribing above it, "This is Gaius' funeral."

poems.title: A Labour of Hercules (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Tiny Macron was found asleep one summer day by a mouse, who pulled him by his tiny foot into its hole; but in the hole he strangled the mouse with his naked hands and cried, "Father Zeus, thou hast a second Heracles."

poems.title: Erotion (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Small Erotion while playing was carried aloft by a gnat, and cried, "What can I do, Father Zeus, if thou dost claim me?"

poems.title: Artemidora (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Fanning thin Artemidora in her sleep, Demetrius blew her clean out of the house.

poems.title: The Atomic Theory (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Epicurus wrote that the whole universe consisted of atoms, thinking, Alcimus, that the atom was the least of things. But if Diophantus had lived then, he would have written, "consisted of Diophantus," who is much more minute than even the atoms, or would have written that all other things indeed consist of atoms, but the atoms themselves of him.

poems.title: Chaeremon (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Borne up by a slight breeze, Chaeremon floated through the clear air, far lighter than chaff, and probably would have gone spinning off through ether, but that he caught his feet in a spider's web, and dangled there on his back; there he hung five nights and days, and on the sixth came down by a strand of the web.

poems.title: A Deadly Dream (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Diophantus, having seen Hermogenes the physician in sleep, never awoke again, though he wore an amulet.

poems.title: The Wise Prophet (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: All the astrologers as from one mouth prophesied to my father that his brother would reach a great old age; Hermocleides alone said he was fated to die early; and he said so, when we were mourning over his corpse in-doors.

poems.title: The Wooden Horse (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: You have a Thessalian horse, Erasistratus, but the drugs of all Thessaly cannot make him go; the real wooden horse, that if Trojans and Greeks had all pulled together, would never have entered at the Scaean gate; set it up as an offering to some god, if you take my advice, and make gruel for your little children with its barley.

poems.title: A Mysterious Disappearance (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Antiochus once set eyes on Lysimachus' cushion, and Lysimachus never set eyes on his cushion again.

poems.title: The Miser and the Mouse (Mackail)
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Asclepiades the miser saw a mouse in his house, and said, "What do you want with me, my very dear mouse?" and the mouse, smiling sweetly, replied, "Do not be afraid, my friend; we do not ask board from you, only lodging."

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.166: εἰκόνα τῆς κήλης Διονύσιος ὧδʼ ἀνέθηκεν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἰκόνα τῆς κήλης Διονύσιος ὧδʼ ἀνέθηκεν,
σωθεὶς ἐκ ναυτῶν τεσσαράκοντα μόνος·
τοῖς μηροῖς αὐτὴν γὰρ ὑπερδήσας ἐκολύμβα.
ἔστʼ οὖν καὶ κήλης ἔν τισιν εὐτυχίη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.10: τὸν τοῦ δειπναρίου νόμον οἴδατε· σήμερον
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν τοῦ δειπναρίου νόμον οἴδατε· σήμερον ὑμᾶς,
Αὖλε, καλῶ καινοῖς δόγμασι συμποσίου.
οὐ μελοποιὸς ἐρεῖ κατακείμενος· οὔτε παρέξεις
οὔθʼ ἕξεις αὐτὸς πράγματα γραμματικά.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.11: οὐκ ᾔδειν σε τραγῳδόν, Ἐπίκρατες, οὐδὲ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐκ ᾔδειν σε τραγῳδόν, Ἐπίκρατες, οὐδὲ χοραύλην,
οὐδʼ ἄλλʼ οὐδὲν ὅλως, ὧν χορὸν ἔστιν ἔχειν
ἀλλʼ ἐκάλουν σε μόνον σὺ δʼ ἔχων χορὸν οἴκοθεν ἥκεις
ὀρχηστῶν, αὐτοῖς πάντα διδοὺς ὀπίσω.
εἰ δʼ οὕτω τοῦτʼ ἐστί, σὺ τοὺς δούλους κατάκλινον,
ἡμεῖς δʼ αὖ τούτοις πρὸς πόδας ἐρχόμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.68: τὰς τρίχας, ὦ Νίκυλλα, τινὲς βάπτειν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὰς τρίχας, ὦ Νίκυλλα, τινὲς βάπτειν σε λέγουσιν,
ἃς σὺ μελαινοτάτας ἐξ ἀγορᾶς ἐπρίω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.69: τὰς πολιὰς βάψασα Θεμιστονόη τρικόρωνος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὰς πολιὰς βάψασα Θεμιστονόη τρικόρωνος
γίνεται ἐξαπίνης οὐ νέα, ἀλλὰ Ῥέα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.75: οὗτος ὁ νῦν τοιοῦτος Ὀλυμπικὸς εἶχε
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὗτος ὁ νῦν τοιοῦτος Ὀλυμπικὸς εἶχε, Σεβαστέ,
ῥῖνα, γένειον, ὀφρῦν, ὠτάρια, βλέφαρα·
εἶτʼ ἀπογραψάμενος πύκτης ἀπολώλεκε πάντα,
ὥστʼ ἐκ τῶν πατρικῶν μηδὲ λαβεῖν τὸ μέρος·
εἰκόνιον γὰρ ἀδελφὸς ἔχων προενήνοχεν αὐτοῦ,
καὶ κέκριτʼ ἀλλότριος, μηδὲν ὅμοιον ἔχων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.76: ῥύγχος ἔχων τοιοῦτον, Ὀλυμπικέ, μήτʼ ἐπὶ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ῥύγχος ἔχων τοιοῦτον, Ὀλυμπικέ, μήτʼ ἐπὶ κρήνην
ἔλθῃς, μήτʼ ἐνόρα πρός τι διαυγὲς ὕδωρ.
καὶ σὺ γάρ, ὡς Νάρκισσος, ἰδὼν τὸ πρόσωπον ἐναργές,
τεθνήξῃ, μισῶν σαυτὸν ἕως θανάτου,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.77: Εἰκοσέτους σωθέντος Ὀδυσσέος εἰς τὰ πατρῷα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Εἰκοσέτους σωθέντος Ὀδυσσέος εἰς τὰ πατρῷα
ἔγνω τὴν μορφὴν Ἄργος ἰδὼν ὁ κύων·
ἀλλὰ σὺ πυκτεύσας, Στρατοφῶν, ἐπὶ τέσσαρας ὥρας,
οὐ κυσὶν ἄγνωστος, τῇ δὲ πόλει γέγονας.
ἢν ἐθέλῃς τὸ πρόσωπον ἰδεῖν ἐς ἔσοπτρον ἑαυτοῦ,
οὐκ εἰμὶ Στρατοφῶν, αὐτὸς ἐρεῖς ὀμόσας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.78: κόσκινον ἡ κεφαλή σου, Ἀπολλόφανες, γεγένηται
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
κόσκινον ἡ κεφαλή σου, Ἀπολλόφανες, γεγένηται,
ἢ τῶν σητοκόπων βιβλαρίων τὰ κάτω·
ὄντως μυρμήκων τρυπήματα λοξὰ καὶ ὀρθά,
γράμματα τῶν λυρικῶν Λύδια καὶ Φρύγια.
πλὴν ἀφόβως πύκτευε· καὶ ἢν τρωθῇς γὰρ ἄνωθεν,
ταῦθʼ ὅσ’ ἔχεις, ἕξεις· πλείονα δʼ οὐ δύνασαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.79: πύκτης ὢν κατέλυσε Κλεόμβροτος· εἶτα γαμήσας
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πύκτης ὢν κατέλυσε Κλεόμβροτος· εἶτα γαμήσας
ἔνδον ἔχει πληγῶν Ἴσθμια καὶ Νέμεα,
γραῦν μαχίμην, τύπτουσαν Ὀλύμπια, καὶ τὰ παρʼ αὐτῷ
μᾶλλον ἰδεῖν φρίσσων ἤ ποτε τὸ στάδιον.
ἂν γὰρ ἀναπνεύσῃ, δέρεται τὰς παντὸς ἀγῶνος
πληγάς, ὡς ἀποδῷ· κἂν ἀποδῷ, δέρεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.80: οἱ συναγωνισταὶ τὸν πυγμάχον ἐνθάδʼ ἔθηκαν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οἱ συναγωνισταὶ τὸν πυγμάχον ἐνθάδʼ ἔθηκαν
Ἆπιν οὐδένα γὰρ πώποτʼ ἐτραυμάτισεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.81: πᾶσαν ὅσαν Ἕλληνες ἀγωνοθετοῦσιν ἅμιλλαν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πᾶσαν ὅσαν Ἕλληνες ἀγωνοθετοῦσιν ἅμιλλαν
πυγμῆς, Ἀνδρόλεως πᾶσαν ἀγωνισάμαν
ἔσχον δʼ ἐν Πίσῃ μὲν ἓν ὠτίον, ἐν δὲ Πλαταιαῖς
ἓν βλέφαρον· Πυθοῖ δʼ ἄπνοος ἐκφέρομαι·
Δαμοτέλης δʼ ὁ πατὴρ καρύσσετο σὺν πολιήταις
ἆραί με σταδίων ἢ νεκρὸν ἢ κολοβόν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.83: τὸν σταδιῆ πρῴην Ἐρασίστρατον ἡ μεγάλη
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν σταδιῆ πρῴην Ἐρασίστρατον ἡ μεγάλη γῆ,
πάντων σειομένων, οὐκ ἐσάλευσε μόνον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.84: οὔτε τάχιον ἐμοῦ τις ἐν ἀντιπάλοισιν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὔτε τάχιον ἐμοῦ τις ἐν ἀντιπάλοισιν ἔπιπτεν,
οὔτε βράδιον ὅλως ἔδραμε τὸ στάδιον
δίσκῳ μὲν γὰρ ὅλως οὐδʼ ἤγγισα, τοὺς δὲ πόδας μου
ἐξᾶραι πηδῶν ἴσχυον οὐδέποτε·
κυλλὸς δʼ ἠκόντιζεν ἀμείνονα· πέντε δʼ ἀπʼ ἄθλων
πρῶτος ἐκηρύχθην πεντετριαζόμενος,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.85: νύκτα μέσην ἐποίησε τρέχων ποτὲ Μάρκος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
νύκτα μέσην ἐποίησε τρέχων ποτὲ Μάρκος ὁπλίτης,
ὥστʼ ἀποκλεισθῆναι πάντοθε τὸ στάδιον.
οἱ γὰρ δημόσιοι κεῖσθαί τινα πάντες ἔδοξαν
ὁπλίτην τιμῆς εἵνεκα τῶν λιθίνων.
καὶ τί γάρ; εἰς ὥρας ἠνοίγετο· καὶ τότε Μάρκος
ἦλθε, προσελλείπων τῷ σταδίῳ στάδιον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.87: Τιμόμαχον τὸν μακρὸν ὁ πεντόργυιος ἐχώρει
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Τιμόμαχον τὸν μακρὸν ὁ πεντόργυιος ἐχώρει
οἶκος, ὑπὲρ γαίης πάντοτε κεκλιμένον
στῆναι δʼ εἲ ποτʼ ἔχρῃζεν, ἔδει τοὺς παῖδας ἀπʼ ὄρθρου
τὴν ὀροφὴν τρῆσαι πέντʼ ἐπὶ πέντε πόδας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.88: τὴν μικρὴν παίζουσαν Ἐρώτιον ἥρπασε κώνωψ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὴν μικρὴν παίζουσαν Ἐρώτιον ἥρπασε κώνωψ·
ἡ δέ· τί, φησί, πάθω; Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἦ μʼ ἐθέλεις

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.89: ὁ βραχὺς Ἑρμογένης, ὅταν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ὁ βραχὺς Ἑρμογένης, ὅταν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς τὸ χαμαί τι,
ἕλκει πρὸς τὰ κάτω τοῦτο δορυδρεπάνῳ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.90: τῷ πατρὶ θυμωθείς, Διονύσιε, Μάρκος ὁ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τῷ πατρὶ θυμωθείς, Διονύσιε, Μάρκος ὁ μικρός,
πυρῆνα στήσας, αὑτὸν ἀπηγχόνισεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.91: ἐν καλάμῳ πήξας ἀθέρα Στρατόνικος ὁ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἐν καλάμῳ πήξας ἀθέρα Στρατόνικος ὁ λεπτός,
καὶ τριχὸς ἐκδήσας, αὑτὸν ἀπηγχόνισεν
καὶ τί γάρ; οὐχὶ κάτω βρῖσεν βαρύς· ἀλλʼ ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν,
νηνεμίας οὔσης, νεκρὸς ἄνω πέταται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.92: Γάιος ἐκπνεύσας τὸ πανύστατον ἐχθὲς ὁ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Γάιος ἐκπνεύσας τὸ πανύστατον ἐχθὲς ὁ λεπτὸς
εἰς τὴν ἐκκομιδὴν οὐδὲν ἀφῆκεν ὅλως·
καὶ πέρας εἰς ἀίδην καταβὰς οἷόσπερ ὅτʼ ἔζη,
τῶν ὑπὸ γῆν σκελετῶν λεπτότατος πέταται.
τὴν δὲ κενὴν κλίνην οἱ φράτορες ἦραν ἐπʼ ὤμων,
ἐγγράψαντες ἄνω· Γάιος ἐκφέρεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.93: τῶν Ἐπικουρείων ἀτόμων ποτὲ Μάρκος ὁ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τῶν Ἐπικουρείων ἀτόμων ποτὲ Μάρκος ὁ λεπτός,
τῇ κεφαλῇ τρήσας, εἰς τὸ μέσον διέβη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.94: Σαλπίζων ἔπνευσεν ὅσον βραχὺ Μάρκος ὁ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Σαλπίζων ἔπνευσεν ὅσον βραχὺ Μάρκος ὁ λεπτός,
καὶ κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς ὀρθὸς ἀπῆλθε κάτω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.95: τὸν μικρὸν Μάκρωνα θέρους κοιμώμενον εὑρὼν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν μικρὸν Μάκρωνα θέρους κοιμώμενον εὑρὼν
εἰς τρώγλην μικρὸς τοῦ ποδὸς εἵλκυσε μῦς.
ὃς δʼ ἐν τῇ τρώγλῃ ψιλὸς τὸν μῦν ἀποπνίξας,
Ζεῦ πάτερ, εἶπεν, ἔχεις δεύτερον Ἡρακλέα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.99: τὸν λεπτὸν φυσῶντα τὸ πῦρ Πρόκλον
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν λεπτὸν φυσῶντα τὸ πῦρ Πρόκλον ἦρεν ὁ καπνός,
καὶ διὰ τῶν θυρίδων ἔνθεν ἀπῆλθεν ἔχων.
ἀλλὰ μόλις νεφέλῃ προσενήξατο, καὶ διʼ ἐκείνης
προσκατέβη τρωθεὶς μυρία ταῖς ἀτόμοις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.100: οὕτω κουφότατος πέλε Γάιος, ὥστʼ ἐκολύμβα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὕτω κουφότατος πέλε Γάιος, ὥστʼ ἐκολύμβα
τοῦ ποδὸς ἐκκρεμάσας ἢ λίθον ἢ μόλιβον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.101: ῥιπίζων ἐν ὕπνοις Δημήτριος Ἀρτεμιδώραν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ῥιπίζων ἐν ὕπνοις Δημήτριος Ἀρτεμιδώραν
τὴν λεπτήν, ἐκ τοῦ δώματος ἐξέβαλεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.103: ἐξ ἀτόμων Ἐπίκουρος ὅλον τὸν κόσμον
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἐξ ἀτόμων Ἐπίκουρος ὅλον τὸν κόσμον ἔγραψεν
εἶναι, τοῦτο δοκῶν, Ἄλκιμε, λεπτότατον.
εἰ δὲ τότʼ ἦν Διόφαντος, ἔγραψεν ἂν ἐκ Διοφάντου,
τοῦ καὶ τῶν ἀτόμων πουλύ τι λεπτοτέρου,
ἢ τὰ μὲν ἄλλʼ ἔγραψε συνεστάναι ἐξ ἀτόμων ἄν,
ἐκ τούτου δʼ αὐτάς, Ἄλκιμε, τὰς ἀτόμους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.104: ἱππεύων μύρμηκι Μενέστρατος, ὡς ἐλέφαντι
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἱππεύων μύρμηκι Μενέστρατος, ὡς ἐλέφαντι,
δύσμορος ἐξαπίνης ὕπτιος ἐξετάθη,
λακτισθεὶς δʼ ὡς εἶχε τὸ καίριον, ὦ φθόνε, φησίν,
οὕτως ἱππεύων ὤλετο καὶ Φαέθων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.105: τὸν μέγαν ἐζήτουν Εὐμήκιον ὃς δʼ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν μέγαν ἐζήτουν Εὐμήκιον ὃς δʼ ἐκάθευδεν
μικρῷ ὑπʼ ὀξυβάφῳ τὰς χέρας ἐκτανύσας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.106: ἀρθεὶς ἐξ αὔρης λεπτῆς ἐποτᾶτο διʼ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἀρθεὶς ἐξ αὔρης λεπτῆς ἐποτᾶτο διʼ αἴθρης
Χαιρήμων, ἀχύρου πολλὸν ἐλαφρότερος·
καὶ τάχʼ ἂν ἐρροίζητο διʼ αἰθέρος, εἰ μὴ ἀράχνῃ
τοὺς πόδας ἐμπλεχθεὶς ὕπτιος ἐκρέματο.
αὐτοῦ δὴ νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα πέντε κρεμασθεὶς
ἑκταῖος κατέβη νήματι τῆς ἀράχνης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.107: αἰγείρου φύλλῳ πεφορημένῳ ἐξ ἀνέμοιο
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
αἰγείρου φύλλῳ πεφορημένῳ ἐξ ἀνέμοιο
πληγεὶς Χαιρήμων ὕπτιος ἐξετάθη.
κεῖται δʼ ἢ Τιτυῷ ἐναλίγκιος, ἢ πάλι κάμπῃ,
ἁπλώσας κατὰ γῆς σῶμα τὸ καννάβινον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.131: οὔτʼ ἐπὶ Δευκαλίωνος ὕδωρ, ὅτε πάντʼ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὔτʼ ἐπὶ Δευκαλίωνος ὕδωρ, ὅτε πάντʼ ἐγενήθη,
οὔθʼ ὁ καταπρήσας τοὺς ἐπὶ γῆς Φαέθων,
ἀνθρώπους ἔκτεινεν ὅσους Ποτάμων ὁ ποιητὴς,
καὶ χειρουργήσας ὤλεσεν Ἑρμογένης.
ὥστʼ ἐξ αἰῶνος κακὰ τέσσαρα ταῦτʼ ἐγενήθη,
Δευκαλίων, Φαέθων, Ἑρμογένης, Ποτάμων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.132: μισῶ, δέσποτα Καῖσαρ, ὅσοις νέος οὐδέποτʼ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
μισῶ, δέσποτα Καῖσαρ, ὅσοις νέος οὐδέποτʼ οὐδεὶς
ἤρεσε, κἂν εἴπῃ, μῆνιν ἄειδε θεά,
ἀλλʼ ἢν μὴ Πριάμου τις ἔχῃ χρόνον ἡμιφάλακρος,
ἢ καὶ κυρτὸς ἄγαν, οὐ δύνατʼ ἄλφα γράφειν.
εἰ δʼ ὄντως οὕτως τοῦτʼ ἔστʼ ἔχον, ὦ ὕπατε Ζεῦ,
εἰς τοὺς κηλήτας ἔρχεται ἡ σοφία.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.133: τέθνηκʼ Εὐτυχίδης ὁ μελογράφος. οἱ κατὰ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τέθνηκʼ Εὐτυχίδης ὁ μελογράφος. οἱ κατὰ γαῖαν
φεύγετʼ ἔχων ᾠδὰς ἔρχεται Εὐτυχίδης·
καὶ κιθάρας αὑτῷ διετάξατο συγκατακαῦσαι
δώδεκα, καὶ κίστας εἰκοσιπέντε νόμων.
νῦν ὑμῖν ὁ Χάρων ἐπελήλυθε· ποῦ τις ἀπέλθῃ
λοιπόν, ἐπεὶ χᾄδην Εὐτυχίδης κατέχει;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.134: Ἀρχόμεθʼ, Ἡλιόδωρε; ποιήματα παίζομεν οὕτω
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Ἀρχόμεθʼ, Ἡλιόδωρε; ποιήματα παίζομεν οὕτω
ταῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους; Ἡλιόδωρε, θέλεις;
ἆσσον ἴθʼ, ὥς κεν θᾶσσον ὀλέθρου καὶ γὰρ ἔμʼ ὄψει
μακροφλυαρητὴν Ἡλιοδωρότερον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.135: μηκέτι, μηκέτι, Μάρκε, τὸ παιδίον, ἀλλʼ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
μηκέτι, μηκέτι, Μάρκε, τὸ παιδίον, ἀλλʼ ἐμὲ κόπτου
τὸν πολὺ τοῦ παρὰ σοὶ νεκρότερον τεκνίου,
εἰς ἐμὲ νῦν ἐλέγους ποίει πάλιν, εἰς ἐμὲ θρήνους,
δήμιε, τὸν στιχίνῳ σφαζόμενον θανάτῳ,
τοῦ σοῦ γὰρ πάσχω νεκροῦ χάριν, οἷα πάθοιεν
οἱ καταδείξαντες βιβλία καὶ καλάμους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.136: οὐχ οὕτω κακοεργὸν ἐχαλκεύσαντο μάχαιραν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐχ οὕτω κακοεργὸν ἐχαλκεύσαντο μάχαιραν
ἄνθρωποι, διὰ τὰς ἐξαπίνης ἐνέδρας,
οἷον ἀκήρυκτον, Καλλίστρατε, καὶ σὺ προσελθὼν
ποιεῖς μοι φονικῶν ἑξαμέτρων πόλεμον.
σάλπιγξον ταχέως ἀνακλητικὸν εἰς ἀνοχὰς γὰρ
καὶ Πρίαμος κλαύσας % ἡμερίων ἔτυχεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.137: Ὠμοβοείου μοι παραθεὶς τόμον, Ἡλιόδωρε
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Ὠμοβοείου μοι παραθεὶς τόμον, Ἡλιόδωρε,
καὶ τρία μοι κεράσας ὠμοβοειότερα,
εὐθὺ κατακλύζεις ἐπιγράμμασιν. εἰ δʼ ἀσεβήσας
βεβρώκειν τινὰ βοῦν τῶν ἀπὸ Τρινακρίας,
βούλομʼ ἅπαξ πρὸς κῦμα χανεῖν εἰ δʼ ἐστὶ τὸ κῦμα
ἔνθε μακράν, ἄρας εἰς τὸ φρέαρ με βάλε.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.138: ἂν τοῦ γραμματικοῦ μνησθῶ μόνον Ἡλιοδώρου
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἂν τοῦ γραμματικοῦ μνησθῶ μόνον Ἡλιοδώρου,
εὐθὺ σολοικίζον τὸ στόμα μου δέδεται,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.139: γραμματικὸν Ζηνωνὶς ἔχει πώγωνα Μένανδρον
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
γραμματικὸν Ζηνωνὶς ἔχει πώγωνα Μένανδρον,
τὸν δʼ υἱὸν τούτῳ φησὶ συνεστακέναι.
τὰς νύκτας δʼ αὐτῇ μελετῶν οὐ παύεται οὗτος
πτώσεις, συνδέσμους, σχήματα, συζυγίας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.140: τούτοις τοῖς παρὰ δεῖπνον ἀοιδομάχοις λογολέσχαις
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τούτοις τοῖς παρὰ δεῖπνον ἀοιδομάχοις λογολέσχαις,
τοῖς ἀπʼ Ἀριστάρχου γραμματολικριφίσιν,
οἷς οὐ σκῶμμα λέγειν, οὐ πεῖν φίλον, ἀλλʼ ἀνάκεινται
νηπυτιευόμενοι Νέστορι καὶ Πριάμῳ,
μή με βάλῃς κατὰ λέξιν ἕλωρ καὶ κύρμα γενέσθαι.
σήμερον οὐ δειπνῶ μῆνιν ἄειδε θεά.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.141: χοιρίδιον καὶ βοῦν ἀπολώλεκα, καὶ μίαν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
χοιρίδιον καὶ βοῦν ἀπολώλεκα, καὶ μίαν αἶγα,
ὧν χάριν εἴληφας μισθάριον, Μενέκλεις·
οὔτε δέ μοι κοινόν τι πρὸς Ὀθρυάδαν γεγένηται,
οὔτʼ ἀπάγω κλέπτας τοὺς ἀπὸ Θερμοπυλῶν
ἀλλὰ πρὸς Εὐτυχίδην ἔχομεν κρίσιν ὥστε τί ποιεῖ
ἐνθάδε μοι Ξέρξης καὶ Λακεδαιμόνιοι;
πλὴν κἀμοῦ μνήσθητι νόμου χάριν, ἢ μέγα κράξω·
ἄλλα λέγει Μενεκλῆς, ἄλλα τὸ χοιρίδιον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.142: πολλοῦ δεῖ καὶ σφίν καὶ τρὶς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πολλοῦ δεῖ καὶ σφίν καὶ τρὶς παρʼ ἕκαστα “ δικασταὶ
ἄνδρες,” καὶ λέγε δὴ τὸν νόμον ἐνθάδε μοι,
καὶ ταυτὶ καὶ μῶν καὶ τετταράκοντα καὶ ἄττα
σκεψάμενος, καί τοι νὴ Δία, καὶ μὰ Δία,
ῥήτωρ ἐστὶ Κρίτων, καὶ παιδία πολλὰ διδάσκει·
προσθήσει δʼ αὐτοῖς γρῦ, φαθὶ καὶ μίν ἔτι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.143: οὐ δέχεται Μάρκον τὸν ῥήτορα νεκρὸν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐ δέχεται Μάρκον τὸν ῥήτορα νεκρὸν ὁ Πλούτων,
εἰπών, “ ἀρκείτω Κέρβερος ὧδε κύων.
εἰ δʼ ἐθέλεις πάντως, Ἰξίονι καὶ Μελίτωνι
τῷ μελοποιητᾖ, καὶ Τιτυῷ μελέτα.
οὐδὲν γὰρ σοῦ χεῖρον ἔχω κακόν, ἄχρις ἂν ἐλθὼν
ὧδε σολοικίζῃ Ῥοῦφος ὁ γραμματικός.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.148: μηδὲ λαλῶν πρῴην ἐσολοίκισε Φλάκκος ὁ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
μηδὲ λαλῶν πρῴην ἐσολοίκισε Φλάκκος ὁ ῥήτωρ,
καὶ μέλλων χαίνειν, εὐθὺς ἐβαρβάρισεν,
καὶ τῇ χειρὶ τὰ λοιπὰ σολοικίζει διανεύων,
κἀγὼ δʼ αὐτὸν ἰδὼν — τὸ στόμα μου δέδεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.153: εἶναι μὲν κυνικόν σε, Μενέστρατε, κἀνυπόδητον
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἶναι μὲν κυνικόν σε, Μενέστρατε, κἀνυπόδητον,
καὶ ῥιγοῦν οὐδεὶς ἀντιλέγει καθόλου·
ἂν δὲ παραρπάξῃς ἄρτους καὶ κλάσματʼ ἀναιδῶς,
κἀγὼ ῥάβδον ἔχω, καὶ σὲ λέγουσι κύνα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.154: πᾶς ὃς ἂν ᾖ πτωχὸς καὶ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πᾶς ὃς ἂν ᾖ πτωχὸς καὶ ἀγράμματος, οὐκέτʼ ἀλήθει,
ὡς τὸ πρίν, οὐδʼ αἴρει φορτία μισθαρίου·
ἀλλὰ τρέφει πώγωνα, καί, ἐκ τριόδου ξύλον ἄρας,
τῆς ἀρετῆς εἶναι φησὶν πρωτοκύων.
Ἑρμοδότου τόδε δόγμα τὸ πάνσοφον εἴ τις ἀχαλκεῖ,
μηκέτι πεινάτω, θεὶς τὸ χιτωνάριον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.155: οὗτος ὁ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἀδάμας βαρύς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὗτος ὁ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἀδάμας βαρύς, οὗτος ὁ πάντῃ
πᾶσιν ἐπιπλήσσων, οὗτος ὁ ῥιγομάχος,
καὶ πώγωνα τρέφων, ἑάλω. τί γάρ; ἀπρεπὲς εἰπεῖν
ἀλλʼ ἑάλω ποιῶν ἔργα κακοστομάτων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.159: τῷ πατρί μου τὸν ἀδελφὸν οἱ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τῷ πατρί μου τὸν ἀδελφὸν οἱ ἀστρολόγοι μακρόγηρων
πάντες ἐμαντεύσανθʼ ὡς ἀφʼ ἑνὸς στόματος·
ἀλλʼ Ἑρμοκλείδης αὐτὸν μόνος εἶπε πρόμοιρον
εἶπε δʼ, ὅτʼ αὐτὸν ἔσω νεκρὸν ἐκοπτόμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.160: πάντες ὅσοι τὸν Ἄρην καὶ τὸν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πάντες ὅσοι τὸν Ἄρην καὶ τὸν Κρόνον ὡροθετοῦσιν,
ἄξιοί εἰσι τυχεῖν πάντες ἑνὸς τυπάνου.
ὄψομαι οὐ μακρὰν αὐτοὺς τυχὸν εἰδότας ὄντως
καὶ τί ποεῖ ταῦρος, καὶ τί λέων δύναται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.161: πρὸς τὸν μάντιν Ὄλυμπον Ὀνήσιμος ἦλθεν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πρὸς τὸν μάντιν Ὄλυμπον Ὀνήσιμος ἦλθεν ὁ πύκτης,
εἰ μέλλει γηρᾶν βουλόμενος προμαθεῖν.
κἀκεῖνος, ναί, φησίν “ ἐὰν ἤδη καταλύσῃς·
ἂν δέ γε πυκτεύῃς, ὡροθετεῖ σε Κρόνος.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.163: πρὸς τὸν μάντιν Ὄλυμπον Ὀνήσιμος ἦλθʼ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πρὸς τὸν μάντιν Ὄλυμπον Ὀνήσιμος ἦλθʼ ὁ παλαιστὴς,
καὶ πένταθλος Ὕλας, καὶ σταδιεὺς Μενεκλῆς,
τίς μέλλει νικᾶν αὐτῶν τὸν ἀγῶνα θέλοντες
γνῶναι. κἀκεῖνος τοῖς ἱεροῖς ἐνιδών,
πάντες, ἔφη, “ νικᾶτε, μόνον μή τις σὲ παρέλθῃ,
καὶ σὲ καταστρέψῃ, καὶ σὲ παρατροχάσῃ.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.164: εἶπεν ἐληλυθέναι τὸ πεπρωμένον, αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἶπεν ἐληλυθέναι τὸ πεπρωμένον, αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ
τὴν γένεσιν διαθεὶς Αὖλος ὁ ἀστρολόγος,
καὶ ζήσειν ὥρας ἔτι τέσσαρας· ὡς δὲ παρῆλθεν
εἰς πέμπτην, καὶ ζῆν εἰδότα μηδὲν ἔδει,
αἰσχυνθεὶς Πετόσιριν ἀπήγξατο· καὶ μετέωρος
θνῄσκει μέν, θνῄσκει δʼ οὐδὲν ἐπιστάμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.165: οὐ γλήχωνι Κρίτων ὁ φιλάργυρος, ἀλλὰ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐ γλήχωνι Κρίτων ὁ φιλάργυρος, ἀλλὰ διχάλκῳ
αὑτὸν ἀποσφραίνει, θλιβομένου στομάχου,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.171: θνῄσκων Ἑρμοκράτης ὁ φιλάργυρος ἐν διαθήκαις
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
θνῄσκων Ἑρμοκράτης ὁ φιλάργυρος ἐν διαθήκαις
αὑτὸν τῶν ἰδίων ἔγραφε κληρονόμον.
ψηφίζων δʼ ἀνέκειτο πόσον δώσει διεγερθεὶς
ἰητροῖς μισθοῦ, καὶ τί νοσῶν δαπανᾷ·
ὡς δʼ εὗρε πλείω δραχμὴν μίαν, ἢν διασωθῇ,
λυσιτελεῖ θνῄσκειν, εἶπε, καὶ ἐξετάθη.
κεῖται δʼ οὐδὲν ἔχων ὀβολοῦ πλέον οἱ δὲ τὰ κείνου
χρήματα κληρονόμοι ἥρπασαν ἀσπασίως.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.172: γεννηθὲν τέκνον κατεπόντισεν Αὖλος ὁ κνιπός
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
γεννηθὲν τέκνον κατεπόντισεν Αὖλος ὁ κνιπός,
ψηφίζων αὐτοῦ σῳζομένου δαπάνας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.174: τὰν ἀναδυομέναν ἀπὸ ματέρος ἄρτι θαλάσσας
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὰν ἀναδυομέναν ἀπὸ ματέρος ἄρτι θαλάσσας
Κύπριν ὅλην χρυσῆν ἐχθὲς ἔκλεψε Δίων
καὶ χερὶ προσκατέσυρεν ὁλοσφύρητον Ἄδωνιν,
καὶ τὸ παρεστηκὸς μικρὸν Ἐρωτάριον.
αὐτοὶ νῦν ἐρέουσιν ὅσοι ποτὲ φῶρες ἄριστοι·
οὐκέτι σοὶ χειρῶν εἰς ἔριν ἐρχόμεθα

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.175: τὸν θεὸν αὐτὸν ἔκλεψεν, ὃν ὁρκίζεσθαι
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν θεὸν αὐτὸν ἔκλεψεν, ὃν ὁρκίζεσθαι ἔμελλεν
Εὐτυχίδης, εἰπών οὐ δύναμαὶ σ’ ὀμόσαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.176: τὸν πτανὸν Ἑρμᾶν, τὸν θεῶν ὑπηρέταν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν πτανὸν Ἑρμᾶν, τὸν θεῶν ὑπηρέταν,
τὸν Ἀρκάδων ἄνακτα, τὸν βοηλάταν,
ἑστῶτα τῶνδε γυμνασίων ἐπίσκοπον,
ὁ νυκτικλέπτας Αὖλος εἶπε βαστάσας·
πολλοὶ μαθηταὶ κρείσσονες διδασκάλων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.177: τὸν τῶν κλεπτόντων μανύτορα Φοῖβον ἔκλεψεν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν τῶν κλεπτόντων μανύτορα Φοῖβον ἔκλεψεν
Εὐτυχίδης, εἰπών, “μὴ πάνυ πολλὰ λάλει,
σύγκρινον δὲ τέχνην τέχνῃ, καὶ χείρεσι χρησμούς,
καὶ μάντιν κλέπτῃ, καὶ θεὸν Εὐτυχίδῃ·
τῶν δʼ ἀχαλινώτων στομάτων χάριν αὐτίκα πραθείς,
τοῖς ὠνησαμένοις πᾶν ὃ θέλεις με λέγε.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.178: βουκόλε, τὰν ἀγέλαν πόρρω νέμε, μή
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
βουκόλε, τὰν ἀγέλαν πόρρω νέμε, μή σε Περικλῆς
ὁ κλέπτης αὐταῖς βουσὶ συνεξελάσῃ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.179: εἰ πόδας εἶχε Δίων οἵας χέρας
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἰ πόδας εἶχε Δίων οἵας χέρας, οὐκέτʼ ἂν Ἑρμῆς
πτηνὸς ἐν ἀνθρώποις, ἀλλὰ Δίων ἐκρίθη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.183: τὴν γένεσιν λυποῦντα μαθὼν Κρόνον Ἡλιόδωρος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὴν γένεσιν λυποῦντα μαθὼν Κρόνον Ἡλιόδωρος,
νύκτωρ ἐκ ναοῦ χρύσεον ἦρε Κρόνον,
τίς πρῶτος κακοποιὸς ἐλήλυθε πείρασον, εἰπών,
“ δέσποτα, καὶ γνώσῃ τίς τίνος ἐστὶ Κρόνος·
ὃς δʼ ἄλλῳ κακὰ τεύχει, ἑῷ κακὸν ἥπατι τεύχει·
εὑρών μοι τιμήν, πᾶν ἀνάτελλʼ ὃ θέλεις.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.184: ἐκ τῶν Ἑσπερίδων τῶν τοῦ Διὸς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἐκ τῶν Ἑσπερίδων τῶν τοῦ Διὸς ἦρε Μενίσκος,
ὡς τὸ πρὶν Ἡρακλέης, χρύσεα μῆλα τρία.
καὶ τί γάρ; ὡς ἑάλω, γέγονεν μέγα πᾶσι θέαμα,
ὡς τὸ πρὶν Ἡρακλέης ζῶν κατακαιόμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.185: Ἑλλήνων ἀπέλυε πόλιν ποτέ, δέσποτα Καῖσαρ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Ἑλλήνων ἀπέλυε πόλιν ποτέ, δέσποτα Καῖσαρ,
εἰσελθὼν ᾆσαι Ναύπλιον Ἡγέλοχος.
Ναύπλιος Ἑλλήνεσσιν ἀεὶ κακόν· ἢ μέγα κῦμα
νηυσὶν ἐπεμβάλλων,˘ ἢ κιθαρῳδὸν ἔχων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.189: πέντʼ ὀβολῶν πέπρακεν Ἀπολλοφάνης ὁ τραγῳδὸς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πέντʼ ὀβολῶν πέπρακεν Ἀπολλοφάνης ὁ τραγῳδὸς
πέντε θεῶν σκευήν, Ἡρακλέους ῥόπαλον,
Τισιφόνης τὰ φόβητρα, Ποσειδῶνος τριόδοντα,
ὅπλον Ἀθηναίης, Ἀρτέμιδος φαρέτρην.
οἱ δὲ θεοὶ πὰρ Ζηνὶ καθήμενοι ἐξεδύθησαν
εἰς βραχὺ σιταρίου κέρμα καὶ οἰναρίου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.190: τὸν δασὺν Ἑρμογένην ζητεῖ πόθεν ἄρξεθʼ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν δασὺν Ἑρμογένην ζητεῖ πόθεν ἄρξεθʼ ὁ κουρεὺς
κείρειν τὴν κεφαλήν, ὄνθʼ ὅλον ὡς κεφαλήν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.191: Ἆρες Ἄρες βροτολοιγέ, μιαιφόνε, παύεο, κουρεῦ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Ἆρες Ἄρες βροτολοιγέ, μιαιφόνε, παύεο, κουρεῦ,
τέμνων οὐ γὰρ ἔχεις οὐκέτι ποῦ με τεμεῖς·
ἀλλʼ ἤδη μεταβὰς ἐπὶ τοὺς μύας ἢ τὰ κάτωθεν
τῶν γονάτων, οὕτω τέμνε με, καὶ παρέχω.
νῦν μὲν γὰρ μυιῶν ὁ τόπος γέμει· ἢν δʼ ἐπιμείνῃς,
ὄψει καὶ γυπῶν ἔθνεα καὶ κοράκων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.192: μακροτέρῳ σταυρῷ σταυρούμενον ἄλλον ἑαυτοῦ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
μακροτέρῳ σταυρῷ σταυρούμενον ἄλλον ἑαυτοῦ
ὁ φθονερὸς Διοφῶν ἐγγὺς ἰδὼν ἐτάκη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.194: Πανὶ φιλοσπήλυγγι καὶ οὐρεοφοιτάσι Νύμφαις
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Πανὶ φιλοσπήλυγγι καὶ οὐρεοφοιτάσι Νύμφαις,
καὶ Σατύροις, ἱεραῖς τʼ ἔνδον Ἁμαδρυάσιν,
σὺν κυσὶ καὶ λόγχαις συοφόντισι Μάρκος
μηδὲν ἑλὼν, αὐτοὺς τοὺς κύνας ἐκρέμασεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.196: ῥύγχος ἔχουσα Βιτὼ τριπιθήκινον, οἷον ἰδοῦσαν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ῥύγχος ἔχουσα Βιτὼ τριπιθήκινον, οἷον ἰδοῦσαν
τὴν Ἑκάτην αὑτὴν οἴομʼ ἀπαγχονίσαι,
εἰμί, λέγει, σώφρων, Λουκίλλιε, καὶ μονοκοιτῶ.
αἰδεῖται, γάρ ἴσως, παρθένος εἰμί, λέγειν.
εἰ δὲ γέ τις μισεῖ με, κακὸν τοιοῦτο γαμήσας,
τῆς αὐτῆς σχοίη τέκνα σαοφροσύνης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.197: ἤθελε ΔΡΙΜΥΣ ἄγαν τὸ πρόσθʼ Ἱερώνυμος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἤθελε ΔΡΙΜΥΣ ἄγαν τὸ πρόσθʼ Ἱερώνυμος εἶναι·
νῦν δὲ τὸ ΔΡΙ μὲν ἔχει, ΛΟΣ δὲ τὸ ΜΥΣ γέγονεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.205: οὐδὲν ἀφῆκεν ὅλως, Διονύσιε, λείψανον Αὔλῳ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐδὲν ἀφῆκεν ὅλως, Διονύσιε, λείψανον Αὔλῳ
Εὐτυχίδης δειπνῶν, ἦρε πάντʼ ὀπίσω·
καὶ νῦν Εὐτυχίδης μὲν ἔχει μέγα δεῖπνον ἐν οἴκῳ,
μὴ κληθεὶς δʼ Αὖλος ξηροφαγεῖ καθίσας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.206: οὕτω σοι πέψαι, Διονύσιε, ταῦτα γένοιτο
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὕτω σοι πέψαι, Διονύσιε, ταῦτα γένοιτο
πάντα· νόμου δὲ χάριν, δός τι καὶ ὧδε φαγεῖν
κἀγὼ κέκλημαι, κἀμοὶ παρέθηκέ τι τούτων
γεύσασθαι Πόπλιος, κἀμὸν ἔπεστι μέρος·
εἰ μὴ λεπτὸν ἰδών με δοκεῖς κατακεῖσθαι ἄρωστον,
εἶθʼ οὕτως τηρεῖς, μή σε λαθών τι φάγω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.207: καὶ τρώγεις ὅσα πέντε λύκοι, Γάμε
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
καὶ τρώγεις ὅσα πέντε λύκοι, Γάμε, καὶ τὰ περισσά,
οὐ τὰ σά, τῶν δὲ πέριξ, πάντα δίδως ὀπίσω.
πλὴν μετὰ τοῦ κοφίνου τοῦ πρὸς πόδας αὔριον ἔρχου,
πρίσματα καὶ σπόγγον καὶ σάρον εὐθὺς ἔχων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.208: ἦν βραδὺς Εὐτυχίδας σταδιοδρόμος· ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἦν βραδὺς Εὐτυχίδας σταδιοδρόμος· ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ δεῖπνον
ἔτρεχεν, ὥστε λέγειν Εὐτυχίδας πέταται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.210: ἄνθρακα καὶ δάφνην παραβύεται ὁ στρατιώτης
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἄνθρακα καὶ δάφνην παραβύεται ὁ στρατιώτης
Αὖλος, ἀποσφίγξας μήλινα λωμάτια.
φρίσσει καὶ τὸ μάτην ἴδιον ξίφος. ἢν δὲ ποτʼ εἴπῃς,
ἔρχοντʼ, ἐξαπίνης ὕπτιος ἐκτέταται.
οὐδενὶ δʼ οὐ Πολέμωνι προσέρχεται, οὐ Στρατοκλείδῃ·
ἀλλὰ φίλῳ χρῆται πάντοτε Λυσιμάχῳ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.211: Γραπτὴν ἐν τοίχῳ Καλπούρνιος ὁ στρατιώτης
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Γραπτὴν ἐν τοίχῳ Καλπούρνιος ὁ στρατιώτης,
ὡς ἔθος ἐστίν, ἰδὼν τὴν ἐπὶ ναυσὶ μάχην,
ἄσφυκτος καὶ χλωρὸς ὁ θούριος ἐξετανύσθη,
ζωγρεῖτε, κράξας, Τρῶες ἀρηΐφιλοι.
καὶ μὴ τέτρωται κατεμάνθανε, καὶ μόλις ἔγνω
ζῆν, ὅτε τοῖς τοίχοις ὡμολόγησε λύτρα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.212: τεκνίον εὔμορφον, Διόδωρε, γράφειν σ’ ἐκέλευσα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τεκνίον εὔμορφον, Διόδωρε, γράφειν σ’ ἐκέλευσα·
ἀλλὰ σύ μοι προφέρεις τεκνίον ἀλλότριον,
τὴν προτομὴν αὐτῷ περιθεὶς κυνός· ὥστε με κλάειν
πῶς μοι Ζωπυρίων ἐξ Ἑκάβης γέγονεν.
καὶ πέρας ἓξ δραχμῶν Ἐρασίστρατος ὁ κρεοπώλης
ἐκ τῶν Ἰσείων υἱὸν Ἄνουβιν ἔχω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.214: γράψας Δευκαλίωνα, Μενέστρατε, καὶ Φαέθοντα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
γράψας Δευκαλίωνα, Μενέστρατε, καὶ Φαέθοντα,
ζητεῖς τίς τούτων ἄξιός ἐστι τίνος.
τοῖς ἰδίοις αὐτοὺς τιμήσομεν ἄξιος ὄντως
ἐστὶ πυρὸς Φαέθων, Δευκαλίων δʼ ὕδατος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.215: εἴκοσι γεννήσας ὁ ζωγράφος Εὔτυχος υἱούς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἴκοσι γεννήσας ὁ ζωγράφος Εὔτυχος υἱούς,
οὐδʼ ἀπὸ τῶν τέκνων οὐδὲν ὅμοιον ἔχει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.216: τὸν φιλόπαιδα Κράτιππον ἀκούσατε· θαῦμα γὰρ
poems.author: Lucillius

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.217: φεύγων τὴν ὑπόνοιαν Ἀπολλοφάνης ἐγάμησεν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
φεύγων τὴν ὑπόνοιαν Ἀπολλοφάνης ἐγάμησεν,
καὶ διὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς νυμφίος ἦλθε μέσης,
αὔριον εὐθύ, λέγων, ἕξω τέκνον. εἶτα προῆλθεν
αὔριον, ἀντὶ τέκνου τὴν ὑπόνοιαν ἔχων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.233: Φαῖδρος πραγματικὸς καὶ ζωγράφος ἤρισε Ῥοῦφος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Φαῖδρος πραγματικὸς καὶ ζωγράφος ἤρισε Ῥοῦφος
τίς θᾶσσον γράψει καὶ τίς ὁμοιότερον.
ἀλλʼ ἐν ὅσῳ Ῥοῦφος τρίβειν τὰ χρώματʼ ἔμελλεν,
Φαῖδρος ἔγραψε λαβὼν εἰκονικὴν ἀποχήν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.234: τοὺς πόδας εἰ Κρατερὸς καὶ τὰς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τοὺς πόδας εἰ Κρατερὸς καὶ τὰς χέρας εἶχʼ ὁλοκλήρους,
οὐκ αὖ τὴν κεφαλὴν εἶχε, τοιαῦτα γράφων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.239: οὔτε Χίμαιρα τοιοῦτον ἔπνει κακὸν ἡ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὔτε Χίμαιρα τοιοῦτον ἔπνει κακὸν ἡ καθʼ Ὅμηρον
οὐκ ἀγέλη ταύρων, ὡς ὁ λόγος, πυρίπνους,
οὐ Λῆμνος σύμπασα, καὶ Ἁρπυιῶν τὰ περισσά,
οὐδʼ ὁ Φιλοκτήτου ποὺς ἀποσηπόμενος·
ὥστε σε παμψηφεὶ νικᾶν, Τελέσιλλα, Χιμαίρας,
σηπεδόνας, ταύρους, ὄρνεα, Λημνιάδας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.240: οὐ μόνον αὐτὴ πνεῖ Δημοστρατίς, ἀλλὰ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐ μόνον αὐτὴ πνεῖ Δημοστρατίς, ἀλλὰ δὴ αὐτῆς
τοὺς ὀσμησαμένους πνεῖν πεποίηκε τράγου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.245: οἱ τοῖχοι, Διόφαντε, τὰ κύματα πάντα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οἱ τοῖχοι, Διόφαντε, τὰ κύματα πάντα δέχονται,
καὶ διὰ τῶν θυρίδων Ὠκεανὸς φέρεται·
δελφίνων δʼ ἀγέλαι καὶ Νηρέος ἀγλαὰ τέκνα
ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ σου νηχόμενα βλέπεται.
ἂν δʼ ἀναμείνωμεν, πλεύσει τάχα καί τις ἐν ἡμῖν
οὐ γὰρ ἔνεστιν ὕδωρ οὐκέτι τῷ πελάγει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.246: ἐκ ποίων ἔταμες, Διονύσιε, τὰ ξύλα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἐκ ποίων ἔταμες, Διονύσιε, τὰ ξύλα ταῦτα
λατομιῶν; ποίων τὸ σκάφος ἐστὶ μύλων;
εἰ γὰρ ἐγώ τι νοῶ, μολίβου γένος, οὐ δρυός ἐστιν,
οὐδʼ ἐλάτης, μικροῦ ῥιζοβολεῖ τὰ κάτω
καὶ τυχὸν ἐξαπίνης ἔσομαι λίθος· εἶτα, τὸ χεῖρον,
γράψει μʼ ὡς Νιόβην δρᾶμα σαπρὸν Μελίτων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.247: ἦ ˘ πέλαγος πλέομεν, Διονύσιε, καὶ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἦ ˘ πέλαγος πλέομεν, Διονύσιε, καὶ γεγέμισται
τὸ πλοῖον παντὸς πανταχόθεν πελάγους.
ἀντλεῖται δʼ Ἀδρίας, Τυρρηνικός, Ἰσσικός, Αἴγων
οὐ πλοῖον, πηγὴ δʼ Ὠκεανοῦ ξυλίνη.
ὁπλίζου, Καῖσαρ· Διονύσιος ἄρχεται ἤδη
οὐκέτι ναυκληρεῖν, ἀλλὰ θαλασσοκρατεῖν,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.249: ἀγρὸν Μηνοφάνης ὠνήσατο, καὶ διὰ λιμὸν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἀγρὸν Μηνοφάνης ὠνήσατο, καὶ διὰ λιμὸν
ἐκ δρυὸς ἀλλοτρίας αὑτὸν ἀπηγχόνισεν.
γῆν δʼ αὐτῷ τεθνεῶτι βαλεῖν οὐκ ἔσχον ἄνωθεν,
ἀλλʼ ἐτάφη μισθοῦ πρός τινα τῶν ὁμόρων.
εἰ δʼ ἔγνω τὸν ἀγρὸν τὸν Μηνοφάνους Ἐπίκουρος,
πάντα γέμειν ἀγρῶν εἶπεν ἄν, οὐκ ἀτόμων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.253: ἐκ ποίων ὁ πατήρ σε δρυῶν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἐκ ποίων ὁ πατήρ σε δρυῶν τέτμηκεν, Ἀρίστων,
ἢ ποίων σε μύλου κόψατο λατομιῶν;
ἦ γὰρ ἀπὸ δρυὸς ἐσσὶ παλαιφάτου ἢ ἀπὸ πέτρης
ὀρχηστής, Νιόβης ἔμπνοον ἀρχέτυπον
ὥστε με θαυμάζοντα λέγειν, ὅτι “ καὶ σύ τι Λητοῖ
ἤρισας· οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἦς αὐτομάτως λίθινος.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.254: πάντα καθʼ ἱστορίην ὀρχούμενος, ἓν τὸ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πάντα καθʼ ἱστορίην ὀρχούμενος, ἓν τὸ μέγιστον
τῶν ἔργων παριδὼν ἠνίασας μεγάλως.
τὴν μὲν γὰρ Νιόβην ὀρχούμενος, ὡς λίθος ἔστης,
καὶ πάλιν ὢν Καπανεύς, ἐξαπίνης ἔπεσες·
ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ τῆς Κανάκης ἀφυῶς, ὅτι καὶ ξίφος ἦν σοι
καὶ ζῶν ἐξῆλθες· τοῦτο παρʼ ἱστορίην,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.256: λούεσθαί σε λέγουσι πολὺν χρόνον, Ἡλιοδώρα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
λούεσθαί σε λέγουσι πολὺν χρόνον, Ἡλιοδώρα,
γραῖαν ἐτῶν ἑκατὸν μὴ καταλυομένην.
πλὴν ἔγνωκα τίνος ποιεῖς χάριν· ὡς ὁ παλαιὸς
ἐλπίζεις Πελίας ἑψομένη νεάσαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.257: Ἑρμογένη τὸν ἰατρὸν ἰδὼν Διόφαντος ἐν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Ἑρμογένη τὸν ἰατρὸν ἰδὼν Διόφαντος ἐν ὕπνοις
οὐκέτʼ ἀνηγέρθη, καὶ περίαμμα φέρων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.258: τῷ Πίσης μεδέοντι τὸ κρανίον Αὖλος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τῷ Πίσης μεδέοντι τὸ κρανίον Αὖλος ὁ πύκτης,
ἓν καθʼ ἓν ἀθροίσας ὀστέον, ἀντίθεται.
σωθεὶς δʼ ἐκ Νεμέας, Ζεῦ δέσποτα, σοὶ τάχα θήσει
καὶ τοὺς ἀστραγάλους τοὺς ἔτι λειπομένους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.259: Θεσσαλὸν ἵππον ἔχεις, Ἐρασίστρατε, ἀλλὰ σαλεῦσαι
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Θεσσαλὸν ἵππον ἔχεις, Ἐρασίστρατε, ἀλλὰ σαλεῦσαι
οὐ δύνατʼ αὐτὸν ὅλης φάρμακα Θεσσαλίης,
ὄντως δούριον ἵππον, ὃν εἰ Φρύγες εἷλκον ἅπαντες
σὺν Δαναοῖς, Σκαιὰς οὐκ ἂν ἐσῆλθε πύλας·
ὃν στήσας ἀνάθημα θεοῦ τινος, εἰ προσέχεις μοι,
τὰς κριθὰς ποίει τοῖς τεκνίοις πτισάνην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.264: ποιήσας δαπάνην ἐν ὕπνοις ὁ φιλάργυρος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ποιήσας δαπάνην ἐν ὕπνοις ὁ φιλάργυρος Ἕρμων
ἐκ περιωδυνίας αὑτὸν ἀπηγχόνισεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.265: εἰ μὲν ἐπʼ ἀττελάβους ἄγεται στρατός
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἰ μὲν ἐπʼ ἀττελάβους ἄγεται στρατός, ἢ κυνομυίας,
ἢ μύας, ἢ ψυλλῶν ἱππικὸν ἢ βατράχων,
Γάιε, καὶ σὺ φοβοῦ μὴ καὶ σέ τις ἐγκαταλέξῃ,
ὡς ἂν τῆς τούτων ἄξιον ὄντα μάχης.
εἰ δʼ ἀρετῆς ἀνδρῶν ἄγεται στρατός, ἄλλο τι παῖζε·
Ῥωμαίοις δʼ οὐδεὶς πρὸς γεράνους πόλεμος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.266: ψευδὲς ἔσοπτρον ἔχει Δημοσθενίς· εἰ γὰρ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ψευδὲς ἔσοπτρον ἔχει Δημοσθενίς· εἰ γὰρ ἀληθὲς
ἔβλεπεν, οὐκ ἂν ὅλως ἤθελεν αὐτὸ βλέπειν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.276: εἰς φυλακὴν βληθείς ποτε Μάρκος ὁ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἰς φυλακὴν βληθείς ποτε Μάρκος ὁ ἀργός, ἑκοντί,
ὀκνῶν ἐξελθεῖν, ὡμολόγησε φόνον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.277: τῆς νυκτὸς τροχάσας ἐν ὕπνοις ποτὲ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τῆς νυκτὸς τροχάσας ἐν ὕπνοις ποτὲ Μάρκος ὁ ἀργός,
οὐκέτʼ ἐκοιμήθη μὴ πάλι που τροχάσῃ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.278: ἔξω παιδεύεις Πάριδος κακὰ καὶ Μενελάου
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἔξω παιδεύεις Πάριδος κακὰ καὶ Μενελάου.
ἔνδον ἔχων πολλοὺς σῆς Ἑλένης Πάριδας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.279: οὐδεὶς γραμματικῶν δύναταί ποτε ἄρτιος εἶναι
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐδεὶς γραμματικῶν δύναταί ποτε ἄρτιος εἶναι,
ὀργήν, καὶ μῆνιν, καὶ χόλον εὐθὺς ἔχων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.295: εἴ τινʼ ἔχεις Διόνυσον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἴ τινʼ ἔχεις Διόνυσον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι τεοῖσι,
τὸν κισσὸν ἀφελὼν, θριδάκων φύλλοις στεφάνωσον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.308: τὸν πόδα τῇ βελόνῃ τρυπῶν Κλεόνικος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὸν πόδα τῇ βελόνῃ τρυπῶν Κλεόνικος ὁ λεπτός,
αὐτὸς ἐτρύπησεν τῷ ποδὶ τὴν βελόνην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.309: Θαρσύμαχε, πλοῦτον πολὺν ὤλεσας ἐξ ἐπιβουλῆς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Θαρσύμαχε, πλοῦτον πολὺν ὤλεσας ἐξ ἐπιβουλῆς,
εἰς οὐδὲν δʼ ἥκεις ἄθλιος ἐξαπίνης,
φεισάμενος, δανίσας, τοκίσας τόκον, ὑδροποτήσας,
πολλάκι μηδὲ φαγών, ὥστε τι πλεῖον ἔχειν.
ἀλλʼ εἴ μοι λογίσαιο τὸ πεινῆν καὶ τότε καὶ νῦν,
οὐδὲν ἔλαττον ἔχεις ὧν τότʼ ἔδοξας ἔχειν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.310: ἠγόρασας πλοκάμους, φῦκος, μέλι, κηρόν, ὀδόντας
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἠγόρασας πλοκάμους, φῦκος, μέλι, κηρόν, ὀδόντας·
τῆς αὐτῆς δαπάνης ὄψιν ἂν ἠγόρασας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.311: οὕτως ἔστʼ ἀργὸς Πανταίνετος, ὥστε πυρέξας
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὕτως ἔστʼ ἀργὸς Πανταίνετος, ὥστε πυρέξας
μηκέτʼ ἀναστῆναι παντὸς ἐδεῖτο θεοῦ.
καὶ νῦν οὐκ ἐθέλων μὲν ἐγείρεται, ἐν δʼ οἱ αὐτῷ
κωφὰ θεῶν ἀδίκων οὔατα μεμφόμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.312: οὐδενὸς ἐνθάδε νῦν τεθνηκότος, ὦ παροδῖτα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐδενὸς ἐνθάδε νῦν τεθνηκότος, ὦ παροδῖτα,
Μάρκος ὁ ποιητὴς ᾠκοδόμηκε τάφον,
καὶ γράψας ἐπίγραμμα μονόστιχον, ὧδʼ ἐχάραξε·
κλαύσατε δωδεκέτη Μάξιμον ἐξ Ἐφέσου.
οὐδὲ γὰρ εἶδον ἐγώ τινα Μάξιμον εἰς δʼ ἐπίδειξιν
ποιητοῦ κλαίειν τοῖς παριοῦσι λέγω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.313: ἀργυρέῃ λιμῷ τις, ἐς εἰλαπίνην με
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἀργυρέῃ λιμῷ τις, ἐς εἰλαπίνην με καλέσσας,
ἔκτανε, πειναλέους τοὺς πίνακας προφέρων.
ὀχθήσας δʼ ἄρʼ ἔειπον ἐν ἀργυροφεγγέι λιμῷ·
ποῦ μοι χορτασίη ὀστρακίνων πινάκων;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.314: ἐζήτουν πινάκων πόθεν οὔνομα τοῦτο καλέσσω
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἐζήτουν πινάκων πόθεν οὔνομα τοῦτο καλέσσω,
καὶ παρὰ σοὶ κληθείς, εὗρον ὅθεν λέγεται.
πείνης γὰρ μεγάλης μεγάλους πίνακας παρέθηκας,
ὄργανα τοῦ λιμοῦ πειναλέους πίνακας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.315: εἴσιδεν Ἀντίοχος τὴν Λυσιμάχου ποτὲ τύλην
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἴσιδεν Ἀντίοχος τὴν Λυσιμάχου ποτὲ τύλην,
κοὐκέτι τὴν τύλην εἴσιδε Λυσίμαχος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.388: ἄχρις ἂν ᾖς ἄγαμος, Νουμήνιε, πάντα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἄχρις ἂν ᾖς ἄγαμος, Νουμήνιε, πάντα δοκεῖ σοι
ἐν τῷ ζῆν εἶναι τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθά·
εἶθʼ ὅταν εἰσέλθῃ γαμετή, πάλιν εὐθὺ δοκεῖ σοι
ἐν τῷ ζῆν εἶναι πάντα κακῶν τὰ κακά.
ἀλλὰ χάριν τεκνίων — ἕξεις, Νουμήνιε, τέκνα,
χαλκὸν ἔχων πτωχὸς δʼ οὐδὲ τὰ τέκνα φιλεῖ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.389: εἰ μὲν ζῇς ἐλάφου ταναὸν χρόνον
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἰ μὲν ζῇς ἐλάφου ταναὸν χρόνον, ἠὲ κορώνης,
συγγνώμη πλεῖστον πλοῦτον ἀγειρομένῳ·
εἰ δὲ τίς ἐσσι βροτῶν, οὓς αὐτίκα γῆρας ἰάπτει,
μὴ σὲ γʼ ἀπειρεσίων οἶστρος ἕλῃ κτεάνων
μὴ σὺ μὲν ἀτλήτοισιν ἐν ἄλγεσι θυμὸν ὀλέσσῃς,
χρήσωνται δʼ ἄλλοι σοῖς ἀγαθοῖς ἀπόνως.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.390: εἴ με φιλεῖς, ἔργῳ με φίλει
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἴ με φιλεῖς, ἔργῳ με φίλει, καὶ μὴ μʼ ἀδικήσῃς,
ἀρχὴν τοῦ βλάπτειν τὴν φιλίαν θέμενος.
πᾶσι γὰρ ἀνθρώποισιν ἐγὼ πολὺ κρέσσονα φημι
τὴν φανερὰν ἔχθραν τῆς δολερῆς φιλίας.
φασὶ δὲ καὶ νήεσσιν ἁλιπλανέεσσι χερείους
τὰς ὑφάλους πέτρας τῶν φανερῶν σπιλάδων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.391: μῦν Ἀσκληπιάδης ὁ φιλάργυρος εἶδεν ἐν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
μῦν Ἀσκληπιάδης ὁ φιλάργυρος εἶδεν ἐν οἴκῳ,
καὶ τί ποιεῖς, φησίν, φίλτατε μῦ, παρʼ ἐμοὶ ;
ἡδὺ δʼ ὁ μῦς γελάσας. “ μηδέν, φίλε, φησί, φοβηθῇς,
οὐχὶ τροφῆς παρὰ σοὶ χρῄζομεν, ἀλλὰ μονῆς.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.392: μύρμηκος πτερόεντος ὑπὲρ νώτοιο καθεσθεὶς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
μύρμηκος πτερόεντος ὑπὲρ νώτοιο καθεσθεὶς
Ἄδραστος ῥήτωρ τοῖον ἔλεξεν ἔπος·
Ἵπτασο· τὸν σὸν ἔχεις, ὦ Πήγασε, Βελλεροφόντην,
φέρτατον ἡρώων, ἡμιθανῆ σκελετόν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.393: οὐκ ἔστιν θυγατρὸς μεῖζον βάρος· εἰ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
οὐκ ἔστιν θυγατρὸς μεῖζον βάρος· εἰ δὲ δοκεῖ σοι,
Εὐκτήμων, εἶναι κοῦφον, ἄκουσον ἐμοῦ.
ἔστιν σοὶ κήλη, κἀμοὶ θυγάτηρ· λάβε ταύτην,
καὶ δός μοι κήλας ἀντὶ μιᾶς ἑκατόν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.164: Γλαύκῳ καὶ Νηρῆι καὶ Ἰνώῳ Μελικέρτῃ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Γλαύκῳ καὶ Νηρῆι καὶ Ἰνώῳ Μελικέρτῃ,
καὶ βυθίῳ Κρονίδῃ, καὶ Σαμόθρᾳξι θεοῖς,
σωθεὶς ἐκ πελάγους Λουκίλλιος ὧδε κέκαρμαι
τὰς τρίχας ἐκ κεφαλῆς· ἄλλο γὰρ οὐδὲν ἔχω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.111: Βουλόμενόσποθʼ ὁ λεπτὸς ἀπάγξασθαι Διόφαντος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Βουλόμενόσποθʼ ὁ λεπτὸς ἀπάγξασθαι Διόφαντος,
νῆμα λαβὼν ἀράχνης αὑτὸν ἀπηγχόνισεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.112: πρίν σ’ ἐναλείψασθαι, Δημόστρατε, χαῖρʼ, ἱερὸν
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
πρίν σ’ ἐναλείψασθαι, Δημόστρατε, χαῖρʼ, ἱερὸν φῶς,
εἰπὲ τάλας· οὕτως εὔσκοπός ἐστι Δίων.
οὐ μόνον ἐξετύφλωσεν Ὀλυμπικόν, ἀλλὰ διʼ αὐτοῦ
εἰκόνος ἧς εἶχεν τὰ βλέφαρʼ ἐξέβαλεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.113: τοῦ λιθίνου Διὸς ἐχθὲς ὁ κλινικὸς
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τοῦ λιθίνου Διὸς ἐχθὲς ὁ κλινικὸς ἥψατο Μάρκος·
καὶ λίθος ὢν καὶ Ζεύς, σήμερον ἐκφέρεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.114: Ἑρμογένην τὸν ἰατρὸν ὁ ἀστρολόγος Διόφαντος
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
Ἑρμογένην τὸν ἰατρὸν ὁ ἀστρολόγος Διόφαντος
εἶπε μόνους ζωῆς ἐννέα μῆνας ἔχειν.
κἀκεῖνος γελάσας, τί μὲν ὁ Κρόνος ἐννέα μηνῶν,
φησί, λέγει, σὺ νόει· τἀμὰ δὲ σύντομά σοι.
εἶπε, καὶ ἐκτείνας μόνον ἥψατο· καὶ Διόφαντος
ἄλλον ἀπελπίζων, αὐτὸς ἀπεσκάρισεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.115: ἤν τινʼ ἔχῃς ἐχθρόν, Διονύσιε, μὴ
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
ἤν τινʼ ἔχῃς ἐχθρόν, Διονύσιε, μὴ καταράσῃ
τὴν Ἶσιν τούτῳ, μηδὲ τὸν Ἁρποκράτην,
μηδʼ εἴ τις τυφλοὺς ποιεῖ θεός, ἀλλὰ Σίμωνα·
καὶ γνώσῃ, τί θεός, καὶ τί Σίμων δύναται,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.116: εἰς Ἄϊδος κατέπεμψε πάλαι ποτέ, δέσποτα
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
εἰς Ἄϊδος κατέπεμψε πάλαι ποτέ, δέσποτα Καῖσαρ,
ὡς λόγος, Εὐρυσθεὺς τὸν μέγαν Ἡρακλέα·
νῦν δʼ ἐμὲ Μηνοφάνης ὁ κλινικός· ὥστε λεγέσθω
κλινικὸς Εὐρυσθεύς, μηκέτι Μηνοφάνης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.408: τὴν κεφαλὴν βάπτεις, τὸ δὲ γῆρας
poems.author: Lucillius
poems.text:
τὴν κεφαλὴν βάπτεις, τὸ δὲ γῆρας οὔποτε βάψεις,
οὐδὲ παρειάων ἐκτανύσεις ῥυτίδας.
μὴ τοίνυν τὸ πρόσωπον ἅπαν ψιμύθῳ κατάπλαττε,,
ὥστε προσωπεῖον, κοὐχὶ πρόσωπον ἔχειν.
οὐδὲν γὰρ πλέον ἐστί· τί μαίνεαι; οὔποτε φῦκος
καὶ ψίμυθος τεύξει τὴν Ἑκάβην Ἑλένην.
